one_line: AI LABS tests Buzz, an open-source group-chat app where Claude and GPT agents share channels; they find real coordination and token-cost problems but praise its per-agent attribution and cross-vendor adversarial review, and say solo builders should skip it.
summary: The AI LABS presenter installs Buzz (a free, open-source "Slack for agents" app, about two weeks old at v0.5) and runs a Claude agent and a GPT/Codex agent in one channel to build a community website. A generic prompt left the agents stalled, tagging each other with no follow-up until nudged; a detailed prompt that assigned roles (Claude plans, GPT reviews) worked. Building was serial and slower than Claude Code's parallel sub-agents. The presenter argues Buzz resends the full conversation on every message while Claude Code already holds that history, so tokens are duplicated and cost scales with each agent. A greeting cost about 31,000 tokens in Buzz versus about 4,000 in the terminal. The highlights are huddles (voice with agents, though Markdown reads poorly aloud), compute sharing across machines, exportable agents with memory, search, and a message ID that ties each action to a named agent. Adversarial review, with GPT attacking a PRD that Claude defends in a shared thread, is the feature they rate best. Their verdict: solo builders should use sub-agents, Claude Code agent teams, or the Codex plugin for Claude Code instead. Teams may find the attribution useful, but there is no end-to-end encryption and no per-channel agent restriction. A mid-video sponsor segment for EgoLite is not evaluated here.

key_ideas.idea: Buzz is a group chat where AI agents are members alongside humans, so agents can hand work to each other directly. Existing options are weaker: Claude Code agent teams run only in the terminal and only Claude agents, and the Claude and Codex Slack integrations only respond when a human mentions them.
key_ideas.detail: The presenter frames the gap as humans carrying every hand-off between agents. Buzz lets Claude Code, Codex and Goose (Dorsey's coding agent) work in one place. The speaker says Claude Tag, Anthropic's Slack agent, is limited to team and enterprise plans.

key_ideas.idea: Each agent gets its own name and login, and every action is recorded under that name. Agents also write linked notes into the shared channel, so every agent can pick up what the others worked out.
key_ideas.detail: The presenter says that if something breaks, you can scroll back to find which agent did it and who asked for it. The speaker calls this the part nobody else has done properly, though it is based on one test run.

key_ideas.idea: Generic prompts stalled the agents; explicit role assignment fixed it. The first prompt tagged both agents with a broad goal, and they went quiet after reviewing each other's plans until the presenter nudged them. A step-by-step prompt that said Claude makes the plan and GPT reviews it coordinated properly.
key_ideas.detail: Build was serial, not parallel: Buzz ran the build tasks one after another, while Claude Code runs several parts at once. The presenter calls this a design problem, not a setting.

key_ideas.idea: Buzz likely duplicates context. It resends the whole conversation on every message while the Claude Code session behind each agent already holds that history, so tokens are spent twice. Each extra agent is its own session, so the cost multiplies rather than adds.
key_ideas.detail: This is the presenter's explanation for an observed gap; it was not verified against Buzz's source. The speaker also cites Anthropic saying agent-team token use grows with the number of agents.

key_ideas.idea: Cost is high even for trivial turns. Answering a greeting used about 31,000 tokens in Buzz, versus about 4,000 for the same message in Claude Code's terminal, with the same context sent.
key_ideas.detail: The presenter's conclusion is that long-running work is expensive in Buzz and that building a product on it is not advised. Their verdict is based on one greeting and one build, so treat the figure as anecdotal.

key_ideas.idea: Adversarial review between different vendors' models is the strongest feature. GPT is told to assume the PRD is wrong and attack it; Claude defends it in a shared thread that both can read. Claude then writes the final plan and asks the user to confirm.
key_ideas.detail: The presenter contrasts this with Claude-only agent teams, where the argument disappears when the session ends. Cross-vendor debate with a persistent, readable thread is the point they say Buzz gets right.

key_ideas.idea: Verdict: solo builders should skip Buzz. Sub-agents, Claude Code agent teams, and OpenAI's Codex plugin for Claude Code (out since March) cover the same use cases more cheaply. For teams, the per-action attribution is the one serious answer, but there is no end-to-end encryption and no way to limit an agent to one channel.
key_ideas.detail: The server operator can read every message, by design, so agents can search the full history. Any agent sees the whole workspace, so private work is not possible yet.

techniques.name: Role-explicit prompt for multi-agent planning
techniques.how: Write a step-by-step prompt that assigns each agent a fixed role, for example Claude writes the plan and GPT reviews it. Name the agents by mention, then give the actual steps. Nudge an agent that stalls with a short update message.
techniques.when: When agents in a shared channel need to coordinate on a plan, and a vague prompt leaves them tagging each other without acting.

techniques.name: Cross-vendor adversarial review of a spec
techniques.how: Mention the attacking agent and tell it to assume the document is wrong (e.g. the PRD). Give the defending agent the opposite brief. Let them argue in one thread. Have the defender write the final plan and ask the human to confirm.
techniques.when: When you want a rival model to catch errors a single-vendor agent team would miss, and you need the debate kept after the session ends.

techniques.name: Per-agent identity and attribution in a shared channel
techniques.how: Give each agent its own name and login. Give every message an ID linked to its sender, so you can trace which agent acted and who triggered it. Search the channel history to find an action.
techniques.when: When several agents act in the same workspace and you need to know which one changed what, and who set it off.

techniques.name: Agent export with memory
techniques.how: Export an agent as a JSON file or PNG. The file carries the agent's accumulated memory, so import it into another instance and the agent keeps what it learned.
techniques.when: When you want to move a configured agent with its memory to another machine or team.

techniques.name: Installing Buzz
techniques.how: Open the GitHub project's latest-releases page, scroll to Assets, and download the installer for your OS. Run it normally. On first launch, either join a community with its link and an invite, or create your own, which is hosted for you. Create agents with Create Agent: name, description (which becomes its instructions), coding tool (Claude Code, Codex, Goose), and model. The app installs Claude Code if missing and asks for one terminal login.
techniques.when: When trying Buzz for a small team. The presenter skipped the self-hosting quick start, which they say is aimed at people who want to host it themselves.

tools: Buzz (v0.5, open-source group-chat app for agents)
Claude Tag (Anthropic Slack agent, team and enterprise plans)
OpenAI Codex plugin for Claude Code

numbers.claim: Buzz gained over 20,000 GitHub stars in its first two weeks.
Buzz offers about 35 models to pick from for the compute-sharing setup.
Answering a simple greeting used about 31,000 tokens in Buzz, versus about 4,000 for the same thing in Claude Code's terminal, with the same context.
Buzz is about two weeks old at version 0.5, per the presenter.
Each new Buzz agent creates its own session with its own context, so the presenter says cost multiplies with the number of agents, not adds up.
Buzz creates three default agents on install.
OpenAI's Codex plugin for Claude Code has been out since March, four months before Buzz existed.
Anthropic's agent-team docs include an example of five agents trying to disprove each other's theories.

hot_takes: The title says Buzz 'fixed' AI agents, but the presenter's own tests show failures in the core selling points, namely coordination, cost and serial building.
Solo builders should not use Buzz; the presenter says sub-agents, Claude Code agent teams, or the Codex plugin for Claude Code do the same work more cheaply and faster.
The per-message attribution record is the one thing the presenter says nobody else has done properly, and is the only real reason they would consider it for a team.
The token-duplication explanation is the presenter's inference from one greeting and one build, not a measured breakdown.
Quality is capped at 2 because of a mid-video sponsor segment (EgoLite, around 7:39 to 9:07), and the title overstates what the test shows.

relevance.why: Per-agent identity and attribution (each message ID tied to a named agent) overlaps AgentOS's Merkle audit log and provenance goals, but this is a single anecdotal test of a chat app, not a pattern to build on.
relevance.action: Check whether AgentOS audit events carry a stable agent identity and the requesting principal, so a trace can show which agent acted and who triggered it.

relevance.why: The cross-vendor adversarial review (Claude defends a PRD, GPT attacks it, in a persistent thread) closely matches ProsHarness's plan to critique (Codex) to debate loop. The video's cost warning applies to it too.
relevance.action: Compare ProsHarness's critique and debate loop with this pattern. Keep the debate in a persistent, readable transcript, and cap the number of rounds to control token cost.
